newsitem.title: UK: Wider Latam Eurobond spreads could hurt borrowers.
newsitem.headline: Wider Latam Eurobond spreads could hurt borrowers.

text.p: Latin American borrowers who did not issue bonds two weeks ago may now be kicking themselves -- a weaker Mexican peso has led to climbing Eurobond yields, and raising debt is now more expensive, traders said on Thursday.
Brazil is a prime example. Roadshows for a $750 million global bond, expected to have a five-year maturity, end on Friday with launch due next week.

Brazilian Brady market debt has come under pressure, with IDU's (Interest Due and Unpaid Bonds) trading at 275 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes compared with 230 b.p. over a few weeks ago, dealers said.

"These falls have to impact the pricing available on the global bond," said an emerging market debt trader. "The question is by how much." "The market is a bit softer, with spreads on benchmark bonds wider. But there has not been any dumping of positions," said Don Pankhurst, emerging market debt trader at WestMerchant Bank.
"Spreads will continue to widen if accounts continue to lighten up on paper," said Nick Blakey, head of emerging market debt trading at UBS.
"Everybody has had a good year, and it is now a case of taking profits and reducing balance sheets before the year-end," he said.
The spread on Mexico's 9.75 percent 2001 dollar bond was quoted at 297 b.p. over U.S. Treasury notes, compared with 284 b.p. over a week ago.
Its 11.0 percent 2026 dollar paper was at 480 b.p. over, 50 b.p. above its all-time low of 430 b.p.
Argentina's 11.0 percent 2006 bond is now at 476 b.p. over compared with 453 b.p. over a week ago.
But the recent weakness should not have come as a real surprise, dealers said.
"People were already expecting the Mexican peso to get to 8.0 to the dollar by the end of 1996," said Blakey at UBS. "But if it gets to 8.25 to the dollar we will see some real nervousness," he said.
The peso closed on Wednesday just above 7.80 per dollar, 30 centavos higher than two weeks ago.
But Eurobonds held by retail investors have not suffered as much, and new issues aimed at this sector may still get tight pricing.
On Wednesday, Argentina launched a 500 million mark 30-year bond at just under five percent over German government paper.
"Softer spreads have only affected some dollar paper, because much of it is held by institutions who trade," said an emerging market debt trader.
"Spreads are steady on bonds held by retail," he said.
One reference point for the upcoming Brazil global is two bonds recently launched by Brazil's state oil company Petrobras.

The five-year tranche, launched at a 250 b.p. spread over Treasuries, has actually tightened to trade at 245 b.p. over. The 10-year tranche was quoted at 365 b.p. over versus a launch spread of 350 b.p. over.
"The Petrobras five-year went very well and was placed very much into retail," said Blakey from UBS.
"The 10-year paper was placed into U.S. institutions and widened because these investors trade more actively," he said.
